meta.title: Who originally recorded "Feeling Good"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a Nina Simone original. "Feeling Good" was written by Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse for the 1964 musical 'The Roar of the Greasepaint', and first performed on stage by Cy Grant. Simone's 1965 version is a cover.
meta.ogDescription: Everyone thinks it's Nina Simone's song. It's a 1964 show tune by Newley and Bricusse, introduced on stage by Cy Grant. Simone's 1965 recording is a cover that eclipsed the original.

answer.label: Not a Nina Simone original — a 1964 stage show tune
answer.originalArtistDates: 1919–2010 · Guyanese-British singer and actor who introduced the song
answer.sourceLine: Almost everyone takes ‘Feeling Good’ for a Nina Simone original, but Simone’s 1965 recording is a cover. The song was written by Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse for the 1964 stage musical The Roar of the Greasepaint – The Smell of the Crowd, and first performed by Cy Grant on the show’s opening night. Simone recorded her version months later and made it so completely her own that the stage origin all but vanished.

original.heading: Where it comes from
original.label: The Roar of the Greasepaint – The Smell of the Crowd (1964 musical)
original.released: Introduced on stage on 3 August 1964 at the Theatre Royal, Nottingham, on the UK tour’s opening night; Cy Grant later recorded a version on his 1965 album Cy & I.
original.charted: Not released as a chart single; the song reached the public through later recordings, above all Nina Simone’s
original.cover: Nina Simone — recorded January 1965, released June 1965 on Philips Records, from I Put a Spell on You. Her reading became the definitive one; later covers by Muse (2001) and Michael Bublé (2005) renewed it for new audiences.

trail: The song was written by Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse for their 1964 musical The Roar of the Greasepaint – The Smell of the Crowd Wikipedia ↗.

Cy Grant was the first to perform it, introducing the number on the UK tour’s opening night in Nottingham on 3 August 1964; he later cut his own version for the 1965 album Cy & I. The point is simply that the song is a show tune, not a Simone composition Cy Grant ↗.

Nina Simone recorded her version in January 1965 for I Put a Spell on You, released that June on Philips, and it became so definitive that most listeners now assume she wrote it — the stage origin, and Cy Grant, largely forgotten the musical ↗.

authors.name: Cy Grant
authors.heading: About Cy Grant
authors.bio: Cy Grant (1919–2010) was a Guyanese-British singer and actor who, in 1964, became the first person to perform ‘Feeling Good’, singing it in The Roar of the Greasepaint – The Smell of the Crowd. He recorded his own version on the 1965 album Cy & I. It is a quiet irony of pop history that he introduced one of the most-covered songs of the era, and almost nobody remembers it was his to introduce.

authors.name: Nina Simone
authors.heading: Why it gets pinned on Nina Simone
authors.bio: Nina Simone (1933–2003) recorded ‘Feeling Good’ in January 1965 for I Put a Spell on You, and her version so completely redefined the song that it is now hers in the public mind. Her reading is genuinely hers and genuinely great; the only error is chronological, the assumption that a song this identified with her must have started with her. It started a year earlier, on a London stage.

authors.name: Anthony Newley & Leslie Bricusse
authors.heading: About Newley & Bricusse
authors.metaLine: British songwriting partnership · wrote the 1964 musical
authors.bio: Anthony Newley (1931–1999) and Leslie Bricusse (1931–2021) were a British songwriting team who wrote ‘Feeling Good’ for their 1964 musical The Roar of the Greasepaint. The same partnership wrote ‘Pure Imagination’ and ‘The Candy Man’ for Willy Wonka and the theme to Goldfinger. They are the figures the song’s fame obscures most: not the famous singer, but the writers whose show tune became a standard.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is the cleanest kind of music misattribution: nothing about Nina Simone’s record is wrong or fake. The only error is believing she originated it — a 1965 cover mistaken for the source, when the source is a 1964 stage musical.

items.why: Simone’s 1965 version is a cover. The song was written a year earlier for a stage musical and first performed by Cy Grant the history ↗.
It was written for The Roar of the Greasepaint – The Smell of the Crowd and premiered on the UK tour in August 1964 the musical ↗.
Grant introduced the song on stage, the earliest performance on record; who cut the very first commercial recording is less clear, but the song plainly predates Simone by a year.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse for a 1964 musical, first performed by Cy Grant, and made famous — but not originated — by Nina Simone in 1965 the record ↗.

context.heading: Why the cover ate the original
lead: Show tunes are unusually prone to this: the stage origin is invisible to radio listeners, who only ever meet the song through a recording. Nina Simone’s arrived early and arrived huge, so it simply became the version, with nothing in the popular memory to displace it.

The irony is that the writers were no obscurity — Newley and Bricusse were a hit theatre-and-film team — yet the song is remembered as Simone’s alone. Each later revival, by Muse in 2001 and Michael Bublé in 2005, only detached it further from a 1964 London stage almost nobody now connects it to.
detailsBody: Newley and Bricusse write ‘Feeling Good’ for The Roar of the Greasepaint (1964).
Cy Grant first performs it on stage, 3 August 1964, on the UK tour.
Nina Simone records her version, January 1965; released June 1965 on Philips.
Simone’s reading becomes definitive, and the stage origin fades from memory.
Muse (2001) and Michael Bublé (2005) revive it for new audiences.
context.pull: A 1964 show tune, introduced on a London stage — remembered as a song Nina Simone wrote.
